name: Occupation traces beside the Gihon Spring
note: Sherds, flint and thin occupation layers found in and around the spring house area. No building plans survive.

name: Early Bronze houses on the eastern slope
note: Kenyon and later excavators found EB I–III sherds and fragmentary walls on the terraces above the spring.

name: Chalcolithic material (redeposited)
note: Chalcolithic finds come mostly from fills and rock pockets, so the size and permanence of any settlement is uncertain.

name: Spring outlet in section
note: The Gihon rises at about 636 m above sea level, low on the eastern flank of the ridge.

name: Spring Tower
note: A tower of boulders up to 3 m across, walls c. 7 m thick, built directly over the spring. Excavated by Reich and Shukron. Traditionally dated to the Middle Bronze Age; radiocarbon evidence published in 2017 permits a late ninth-century BCE construction scenario, though the interpretation is contested — existence and scale are secure, the date is disputed.

name: Rock-cut fortified pool
note: A large reservoir cut into bedrock and enclosed by walls, fed from the spring. Its full depth is still not known.

name: Pool Tower
note: The southern anchor of the Middle Bronze water fortress, protecting the pool.

name: Channel II
note: A rock-cut channel running south along the slope, feeding irrigation outlets in the Kidron valley floor.

name: Middle Bronze fortification line
note: Wall segments on the eastern crest are dated to MB II; the line between them is reconstructed.

name: Warren's Shaft system — upper tunnel
note: The rock-cut passage is probably Middle Bronze; whether the vertical shaft was ever used to draw water is disputed.

name: Extent of the Jebusite town (reconstructed)
note: About 4–5 hectares. Almost no Late Bronze buildings have been found, so the outline follows the fortification line, not walls of houses.

name: Acropolis / rulers' quarter (location proposed)
note: The Amarna letters of Abdi-Heba imply a palace and a garrison, but no Late Bronze palace has been excavated.

name: Stepped terraces beneath the Stepped Stone Structure
note: Kenyon dated the earliest terracing to the Late Bronze Age; others place all of it in the Iron Age. The dating is unresolved.

name: Late Bronze burial finds, Kidron slope
note: Imported Cypriot and Mycenaean pottery from tombs across the valley shows the town was connected to wider trade.

name: Stepped Stone Structure
note: A mantle of stone stepping down the slope, standing about 18 m high — the largest Iron Age structure known in Jerusalem. Its date is argued between the 12th and 9th centuries BC.

name: Large Stone Structure
note: Eilat Mazar identified these walls as King David's palace. Others read them as several separate walls of different dates, or as part of the same fortification as the Stepped Stone Structure.

name: Proto-Aeolic capital (find spot)
note: A carved capital of a type used in royal buildings, found fallen on the slope by Kenyon.

name: Eastern city wall (Iron IIA)
note: Segments on the eastern crest; long stretches are reconstructed between excavated points.

name: Iron IIA buildings on the eastern terraces
note: Fragmentary walls and floors beneath the better-preserved 8th–7th century houses.

name: Hezekiah's Tunnel
note: 533 m of tunnel cut through the ridge from both ends at once, carrying the spring water to the pool at the southern tip.

name: Siloam Inscription (find spot)
note: Found in 1880 near the tunnel's southern exit; it describes the two digging teams meeting. Removed to Istanbul in 1891.

name: Warren's Shaft
note: A natural karstic shaft, about 13 m deep, met by chance by the rock-cut passage. Older books had Joab climbing it to take the city for David (2 Samuel 5:8); Reich and Shukron showed the passage was not originally designed as a bucket-drawing installation at the shaft, substantially weakening the tsinnor identification — the Jebusites more plausibly reached their water through the fortified Spring Tower and rock-cut pool instead.

name: Iron Age pool at the southern tip
note: The tunnel's outlet fed a reservoir at the tip of the ridge, later replaced by the Herodian pool.

name: Broad Wall (western hill)
note: A 7 m thick wall found by Avigad in the Jewish Quarter, showing the city expanded west in the 8th century. It lies off this ridge, to the north-west.

name: Ashlar House
note: A building with dressed-stone corners — unusual quality for a private house.

name: House of Ahiel
note: A four-room house named from a sherd inscribed ""Ahiel""; it had a stone toilet seat in a small side room.

name: Burnt Room
note: Filled with charred wood, including imported furniture timber burnt in 586 BC.

name: Bullae House
note: Fifty-one clay seal impressions were baked hard by the fire that destroyed it, preserving the names of Judahite officials.

name: LMLK jar handles (find spots)
note: Storage jars stamped ""belonging to the king"", linked to Hezekiah's preparations against Assyria.

name: Terrace houses on the eastern slope
note: Dense housing stepped down the slope on artificial terraces, the densest Iron Age quarter yet found here.

name: Destruction layer, Area G
note: Up to a metre of ash, collapsed stone and smashed pottery sealing the Iron Age houses.

name: Arrowheads (Scythian and local types)
note: Bronze and iron arrowheads scattered in the burnt debris, widely associated with the Babylonian conquest of 587/586 BC — artifacts alone do not identify a specific attacker.

name: Collapse of the terrace system
note: Once the houses burned, the terraces they stood on slid down the slope, sealing everything beneath.

name: Contracted Persian-period settlement
note: A small community, perhaps a few hundred people, clustered on the upper ridge. Persian-period remains are thin and often eroded away.

name: Wall attributed to Nehemiah (proposed)
note: Eilat Mazar identified a wall on the crest as Nehemiah's. Critics argue the pottery beneath it is later, or that the wall is Iron Age reused.

name: Seleucid Akra (proposed identification)
note: A massive glacis, tower and slingstones found in the Givati Parking Lot were published in 2015 as the Akra garrison fort. The identification is widely discussed and not settled.

name: Hasmonean fortification and buildings
note: The First Wall of the Hasmonean period ran along the ridge crest and around the southern tip.

name: Yehud and rhodian stamped handles
note: Administrative stamps naming the province of Yehud, plus imported wine-jar handles, are the clearest Persian-Hellenistic evidence.

name: Pool of Siloam (monumental, stepped)
note: Uncovered by accident in 2004 during sewer work. Stepped on at least three sides, more than 60 m along one side, paved and plastered.

name: Monumental stepped street (commonly interpreted as a pilgrimage route)
note: A stepped street about 8 m wide, paved with large slabs. Excavated in sections over some 600 m from the pool towards the Temple Mount; existence and width are secure for excavated segments, and construction after AD 30/31 is secure for the excavated segments; the coins support construction during the governorship of Pontius Pilate. The continuous course drawn here includes reconstructed stretches, and its function as a pilgrimage route is an interpretation, not a measured fact.

name: Drainage channel beneath the street
note: A stone-roofed channel high enough to walk in. Josephus says refugees hid in the drains in AD 70, and cooking pots and coins were found inside.

name: Ritual baths (miqva'ot)
note: Stepped immersion pools cut into bedrock beside the street and in houses — pilgrims purified themselves before going up to the Temple.

name: Mansions attributed to the Adiabene royal house
note: A large, richly built complex in the Givati excavations. Josephus places the palaces of Queen Helena's family here, but nothing found names them.

name: Theodotus synagogue inscription (find spot)
note: A Greek dedication found by Weill in 1913, recording a synagogue built for reading the Law and lodging pilgrims.

name: Late Second Temple houses and shops
note: Shops opened onto the street; behind them stood houses with stone vessels and plastered floors.

name: Destruction debris over the street
note: Collapsed masonry, burnt beams and ash lie directly on the paving stones, with coins of the Revolt sealed beneath.

name: Southern limit of Aelia Capitolina
note: When Hadrian refounded the city in AD 130, the new grid sat north of here. The old ridge was left outside — quarried, farmed and largely empty for two centuries.

name: Quarrying and robbing of the ruins
note: Roman-period pits cut into the ruins to salvage building stone.

name: Siloam Church (attributed to Eudocia)
note: A basilica built over the pool, known from pilgrim accounts and from remains found by Bliss and Dickie in the 1890s. Its attribution to the empress Eudocia rests on written sources.

name: Pilgrimage complex at the pool
note: Courtyards, steps, water channels and lodgings served pilgrims who came to wash in the pool.

name: Byzantine city wall around the ridge
note: A southern wall commonly associated with fifth-century expansion enclosed much of the ridge again; its precise date, builder and full course remain debated, and the attribution to Eudocia rests on written sources rather than an inscription — traced by Bliss and Dickie and confirmed since.

name: Byzantine houses and streets
note: The ridge filled up again — the densest occupation between the Iron Age and the modern village.

name: Umayyad-period buildings
note: Well-built stone buildings with plastered floors, some very large, excavated in the Givati Parking Lot and on the eastern slope.

name: Earthquake-collapse horizon (commonly dated AD 749)
note: Walls found lying flat in one direction, with vessels crushed on the floors beneath — commonly associated with the mid-eighth-century earthquake, often dated to 18 January AD 749.

name: Contraction and abandonment
note: After 749 the ridge was never rebuilt at the same scale; by the 10th century it was mostly fields outside the walled city.

name: Agricultural terracing
note: Stone-walled terraces turned the ruined slopes into orchards and vegetable plots. Many of the ""steps"" visible today are terrace walls, not ancient buildings.

name: Village of Silwan (original core, east of the Kidron)
note: The village grew on the eastern side of the valley, using Iron Age rock-cut tombs as houses and stables.

name: Village spreading onto the ridge
note: From the late Ottoman period houses climbed across the Kidron and onto the ridge itself, directly over the ancient city.

name: Cemeteries and field walls
note: The southern tip stayed open ground — gardens, threshing floors and burial plots.

name: Area G — Kenyon (1961–67) and Shiloh (1978–85)
note: The deep cut through the eastern slope that exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, the Iron Age houses and the 586 BC destruction.

name: Givati Parking Lot excavation (2007– )
note: The largest open excavation on the ridge: layers from the Iron Age to the Abbasid period, including the proposed Akra and the Adiabene mansion.

name: Reich & Shukron — spring and pool (1995–2010)
note: Re-excavation around the Gihon revealed the Middle Bronze water fortress and, in 2004, the Herodian Pool of Siloam.

name: Weill excavation (1913–14, 1923–24)
note: Where the Theodotus inscription and the rock-cut chambers sometimes called the tombs of the kings of Judah were found.

name: Macalister & Duncan (1923–25)
note: They exposed the top of the Stepped Stone Structure and misdated it to the Jebusite and Maccabean periods.

name: Parker Mission tunnels (1909–11)
note: A treasure hunt for the Ark that cleared the ancient water tunnels — badly recorded, but it produced the first plans of the system.

name: Warren's tunnels (1867)
note: Charles Warren mined horizontally into the slope, finding the shaft that carries his name.

name: Bliss & Dickie (1894–97)
note: They tunnelled along the southern city wall, tracing the Byzantine circuit and the church at the pool.

name: Monumental stepped street tunnel excavation (2013– )
note: The street is being dug out beneath the village by tunnelling rather than from the surface — the most contested method used on the site.

name: Archaeological park boundary
note: The visitor site run today over and beneath a living neighbourhood.

name: Wadi Hilweh / Silwan today
note: Several thousand people live directly above the excavations. Residents and some archaeologists contest the digging, the tunnelling beneath houses, and who controls the site.
